title: STP Toolkit: Root Guard
summary: Why root bridge placement matters for traffic flow and reliability, how a switch outside your control can steal the root role, and how Root Guard enforces your root bridge by blocking ports that receive superior BPDUs.

sections.title: Choosing the root bridge is not a random decision

content.body:
STP prevents loops by electing a root bridge and ensuring every other switch has exactly one valid path to reach it. **Any** of the switches could be the root and STP would still prevent loops — but you should not pick one at random. Two things matter:

**Optimal traffic flow** — minimise latency and congestion. *Latency* is how long traffic takes to cross the LAN; *congestion* is how busy the network is. Pumping too much water through a small pipe is inefficient, and the same applies to network links.

**Stability and reliability** — once you have a root bridge that gives an efficient path, you want it to stay up as long as possible. If your LAN mixes switch models, make one of the **more advanced, reliable** switches the root. If you could only afford a couple of new switches and the rest are old junkers from the closet, make a new one the root — you can rely on it not to die after a few weeks.

**Worked example.** SW1 connects to R1, the gateway to the outside world. In most LANs, PCs do not talk to each other much — they talk to servers on the Internet or across the WAN. Making SW1 the root means SW2's hosts use the direct SW2–SW1 link and SW3's hosts use the direct SW3–SW1 link: the most efficient path to R1 for everyone.

Make **SW3** the root instead, and SW2's traffic must go SW2 → SW3 → SW1 before reaching R1. The extra latency is negligible — probably under a millisecond. **The real issue is congestion** on the SW3–SW1 link, which now carries everyone's traffic. On a busy network frames wait their turn and, in the worst case, get dropped.

sections.title: When a switch outside your control steals the root role

content.body:
Inside your own LAN, controlling the root bridge is easy — set its priority to **0**. On a Cisco switch running PVST+ the VLAN ID is always added, so SW1's Bridge ID priority becomes `0 + 1 = 1` in VLAN 1. With SW2 and SW3 at default priority, SW1 is the root.

But sometimes you connect your LAN to switches **outside your direct control**. A common example: a **service provider** offering **Metro Ethernet** to a **customer**. (Metro Ethernet is not a CCNA topic; it is often used to connect sites within a MAN — a metropolitan area network — such as offices in the same city.)

Say the provider made SW1 its root with priority 0, and the customer made SW6 its root with priority 0 too. When the two networks connect, SW2 and SW3 advertise SW1 as root, while SW4 and SW5 advertise SW6. **Who wins?**

SW1 and SW6 have identical priorities (1) and MAC addresses that match up to a point — `52:54:1...`. The next digit is **A** for SW1 and **8** for SW6. SW6 has the lower Bridge ID, so **SW6 becomes the root bridge for both networks.**

The lesson: **even with priority 0, your root's role can be taken by another switch with a lower MAC address.**

The consequence for the provider: SW1, SW2 and SW3 all accept SW6 as root. The SW1–SW3 and SW2–SW3 links get disabled, so frames from SW3 to SW1 must **detour through the customer's LAN**. Clearly unacceptable.

steps.narration: The provider set SW1's priority to 0 so it is the root of their LAN. The customer did the same with SW6 in theirs. Both LANs are happy — separately.
The networks are connected. SW2 and SW3 advertise SW1 as root; SW4 and SW5 advertise SW6. Both claim priority 1.
The MAC addresses break the tie. SW6's is lower, so SW6 wins — a switch outside the provider's control becomes root for both LANs.
The SW1–SW3 and SW2–SW3 links are disabled. Frames from SW3 to SW1 now detour through the customer's network. Unacceptable for the provider.
Root Guard is configured on the provider's customer-facing ports — SW2's G0/2 and SW3's G0/2. When a superior BPDU arrives, those ports go broken / root-inconsistent.
SW1 stays root for the provider LAN. The customer then raises SW6's priority to 4096+1; after about 20 seconds the superior BPDUs age out and the ports recover automatically.

content.body:
**Root Guard prevents a port from becoming a root port by disabling it if superior BPDUs are received**, thereby enforcing the current root bridge.

A **superior BPDU** is one with better parameters for the STP algorithm — most importantly, a **lower root Bridge ID**. SW6's BPDUs claim a lower root Bridge ID than SW1's, so they are superior.

Configure it only on the ports facing switches outside your control:

```
SW2(config)# interface g0/2
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
```

**There is no global command to enable Root Guard by default.** This is deliberate:

- PortFast *can* be enabled by default, because you usually want it on all access ports.
- BPDU Guard and BPDU Filter *can* be enabled by default on all PortFast ports, because they pair with PortFast.
- Root Guard is **not** something you want everywhere. It belongs on specific ports only — hence no global option.

When a Root Guard port receives a superior BPDU it enters the **broken / root-inconsistent** state:

- **`BKN`** in the Status column of `show spanning-tree` = **broken** — the port cannot forward frames and discards anything it receives.
- **`ROOT_Inc`** = **root inconsistent** — the reason it is broken is Root Guard.

A log message also appears confirming Root Guard blocked the port.

While a Root Guard port is blocked, both ends of that link are designated ports — because the two switches disagree about who the root bridge is. In a normal, functioning spanning tree there is only ever one designated port per link. This is a special case caused by Root Guard blocking the link.

sections.title: Recovering a Root Guard blocked port

content.body:
Root Guard solved the provider's problem — but it also means the customer cannot communicate over the provider's network. The fix is to **stop the superior BPDUs**.

The provider tells the customer to raise SW6's priority, say to `4096 + 1` for the VLAN ID. Once the superior BPDUs already received by SW2 and SW3 **age out** — about **20 seconds**, the default max age — the ports are **automatically re-enabled**.

After that, SW4, SW5 and SW6 accept SW1 as the root bridge, and the final topology gives every switch one active path to SW1 with the remaining links blocked.

**The key point: you do nothing in the CLI of the switch running Root Guard.** Unlike BPDU Guard, there is no `shutdown` / `no shutdown` and no errdisable recovery. Just stop the superior BPDUs and the port recovers by itself.

**One more caution:** the **customer** should not configure Root Guard on their ports facing the provider. Those ports would simply be disabled on receiving superior BPDUs, blocking the links — and there is no point connecting to a service provider if you cannot communicate over their network.

rows: **Automatic** once superior BPDUs stop and age out (~20 s)
Ports facing switches outside your control

commands.example:
SW2(config)# interface g0/2
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root
commands.description: Enables Root Guard on the interface. If that port receives a superior BPDU — one that would make the neighbour the root bridge — the port is placed in the root-inconsistent state and stops forwarding.
commands.note: Typically applied by a service provider on ports facing customer switches, to stop a customer accidentally becoming the root of the provider's spanning tree.

commands.syntax: — there is no spanning-tree guard root default —
commands.example:
SW2(config)# spanning-tree guard root
                ^
% Invalid input detected
commands.description: Root Guard deliberately has no global default command. PortFast, BPDU Guard and BPDU Filter can sensibly be enabled everywhere; Root Guard belongs only on specific, chosen ports.
commands.note: A likely exam question: which of these STP features cannot be enabled globally? The answer is Root Guard.

commands.example:
SW2# show spanning-tree
Gi0/2  Desg BKN*4   128.2  P2p *ROOT_Inc
commands.description: Shows a Root-Guard-blocked port with status BKN (broken) and the reason ROOT_Inc (root inconsistent).
commands.note: Broken means the port can neither send nor receive user traffic. Note that both ends of a Root-Guard-blocked link are designated ports — an unusual situation.

commands.description: Used alongside Root Guard to place the root bridge deliberately — ideally on the switch next to the gateway router, for optimal traffic flow and stability.
commands.note: Even priority 0 does not guarantee the root role: with PVST+ the VLAN ID is added to the priority, and ties are broken by the lowest MAC address.

questions.question: What triggers Root Guard to block a port?
questions.explanation: Root Guard reacts only to superior BPDUs — those advertising a better (lower) root Bridge ID. Ordinary BPDUs are fine; that is BPDU Guard's trigger.

options.label: A
options.text: Receiving any BPDU

options.label: B
options.text: Receiving a superior BPDU

options.label: C
options.text: Ceasing to receive BPDUs

options.label: D
options.text: Receiving a BPDU on a trunk port

questions.question: How do you re-enable a port that Root Guard has blocked?
questions.explanation: Nothing is done on the switch running Root Guard. Once the superior BPDUs stop arriving and the stored ones age out — roughly 20 seconds, the default max age — the port recovers automatically.

options.label: A
options.text: `shutdown` then `no shutdown`

options.label: B
options.text: `errdisable recovery cause rootguard`

options.label: C
options.text: Stop the superior BPDUs — the port recovers automatically after about 20 seconds

options.label: D
options.text: Reload the switch

questions.question: Why is there no global command to enable Root Guard by default?
questions.explanation: PortFast, BPDU Guard and BPDU Filter suit blanket enabling because they belong on all host-facing ports. Root Guard belongs only on specific ports facing switches outside your control, so Cisco provides no global option.

options.label: A
options.text: Because it only works on trunk ports

options.label: B
options.text: Because it should only be enabled on specific ports facing switches outside your control

options.label: C
options.text: Because it requires PortFast to be enabled first

options.label: D
options.text: Because it is a per-VLAN feature

questions.question: In `show spanning-tree`, what do the status values BKN and ROOT_Inc mean?
questions.explanation: BKN means broken — the port cannot forward frames and discards what it receives. ROOT_Inc means root inconsistent, identifying Root Guard as the reason.

options.label: A
options.text: The port is blocked, and Root Guard is the reason

options.label: B
options.text: The port is err-disabled by BPDU Guard

options.label: C
options.text: The port is in the Learning state

options.label: D
options.text: The port has a native VLAN mismatch

questions.question: You set your root bridge's priority to 0, so it can never lose the root role. True or false?
questions.explanation: False. If another switch also has priority 0 (or the same effective priority), the MAC address breaks the tie — and a switch outside your control with a lower MAC address can still take over. That is exactly why Root Guard exists.

options.label: A
options.text: True — priority 0 is always the lowest possible Bridge ID

options.label: B
options.text: False — another switch with the same priority and a lower MAC address can still win

options.label: C
options.text: True — but only within a single VLAN

options.label: D
options.text: False — priority 0 is not a valid value

questions.question: In a service-provider / customer Metro Ethernet connection, where should Root Guard be configured?
questions.explanation: On the provider's ports facing the customer. If the customer configured it on their provider-facing ports, those ports would block on receiving the provider's superior BPDUs — leaving the customer unable to use the service at all.

options.label: A
options.text: On the provider's ports facing the customer

options.label: B
options.text: On the customer's ports facing the provider

options.label: C
options.text: On both sides of the link

options.label: D
options.text: On every port in both networks
